name: Columbia Journalism Review: Tow Center Research on AI in Newsrooms
title: Columbia Journalism Review: Tow Center Research on AI in Newsrooms
answer: The Columbia Journalism Review publishes Tow Center research on how news organisations use AI, including a report built on 134 interviews at 35 outlets, a survey of journalists' own AI practices, an analysis of AI tools against journalistic standards, and expert guidance on writing newsroom AI policy. Its most useful contribution is evidence that AI's benefits in news are often mundane and task-dependent, while publishers grow more dependent on the platform companies supplying the technology.

sections.body: The Columbia Journalism Review, published by Columbia University's journalism school, carries reporting and research from its Tow Center for Digital Journalism. The material reviewed spans four pieces: a Tow Center report titled Artificial Intelligence in the News, a CJR feature called How We're Using AI produced with the University of Southern California's AI for Media and Storytelling Initiative, an analysis asking whether AI tools can meet journalistic standards, and a feature gathering expert advice on developing newsroom AI guidelines. The pages carry no single publication date, though the analysis references events into May 2025.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The Tow Center report draws on 134 interviews with news workers at 35 organisations in the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany, among them The Guardian, Bayerischer Rundfunk, the Washington Post, The Sun and the Financial Times, plus 36 international experts. It finds AI adopted under market pressure, competitive dynamics and hype, applied across a widening range of production and distribution tasks. Many of the most beneficial applications are mundane, and AI has often not proved a silver bullet. Efficiency gains, seen in dynamic paywalls, automated transcription and data analysis, are task and context dependent and can be curtailed by unreliable outputs and reputational risk. The report argues AI further rationalises news work and may reinforce publishers' dependency on the technology sector, since larger, better resourced organisations develop AI in house while most others, especially smaller ones, buy third-party platform solutions because of computing costs, competition for tech talent and scarce datasets. The analysis piece reports that common models including ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Meta AI cannot reliably cite sources, and covers attribution disputes involving Perplexity, Forbes and Wired, plus copyright suits against OpenAI and Microsoft.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The report rests on 134 interviews at 35 news organisations and 36 international experts. Ben Welsh of Reuters says roughly a quarter of the code at Reuters is now written by AI. A 2025 Institute for Nonprofit News survey found data analysis, grant application drafting and data scraping among the most common self-reported AI uses among member newsrooms. Most newsrooms with AI policies explicitly ban generative AI for writing and image creation. The New York Times filed its copyright suit in the Southern District of New York in December 2023, and signed an AI licensing deal with Amazon in May 2025.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in media, this source supplies independent evidence rather than vendor claims. It documents what newsrooms actually do with AI, from transcription and dynamic paywalls to satellite imagery analysis, and where gains fail. It maps the dependency relationship between publishers and platform companies, names the copyright battles and licensing deals shaping content supply, and offers practical policy guidance: decide values before writing rules, label significant AI use, keep a human responsible for every published word, and treat plagiarism as a fireable offence.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Media

sections.body: The material is a set of separate pieces rather than one continuous study, and the pages reviewed carry no single date, so some findings may already be overtaken by a fast-moving field. The Tow Center report covers three countries only. The guidance feature reflects the views of named experts rather than a formal standard, and the analysis of AI tools and lawsuits describes disputes that remain unresolved in court.
